Coal accounted for 26.7% of total flows in 2017. The proportion is projected to decrease to 3.2% by 2050. Basic chemicals are expected to increase from 8.2% in 2017 to 15.5% in 2050. Similarly, mixed freight is expected to increase from 13.3% in 2017 to 20% in 2050. 48 Figure 5-13 Proportion of Tons for Major Commodities by Year (2017–2050) Furthermore, to identify the rail corridors with the highest potential for future energy consumption (2025–2050), a two-step approach was employed. First, to assess the trend of tonnage of each rail link, Spearman’s rank correlation coefficient was calculated. This statistical method measures the strength and direction of a trend over time; in this context, a positive coefficient indicates a consistent increase in tonnage. Next, the average tonnage on each link over the specified period was determined. The product of these two values yielded a growth-weighted-tonnage score. This approach allowed the identification of corridors with the greatest potential for increased energy consumption. The key data gaps hindering this assessment include: • Limited data on refueling depot locations: Although the data on state-level fuel consumption by rail is available, further disaggregation is difficult as data on existing refueling depots is limited and often kept private by rail companies. This information gap 50 makes it challenging to strategically locate alternative fueling infrastructure, thereby impeding the development of a comprehensive transition strategy. • Lack of location-specific data on current biofuel availability: While there is some use of drop-in biofuels for the rail sector, it is difficult to ascertain the availability of biofuels (for example, BD and RD) at these locations. This gap makes it difficult to assess the existing infrastructure for these alternative fuels and understand the current capacity for renewable fuel use in the rail sector.
